chapters.title: Units and Measurements
points: SI system has 7 base units: metre (length), kilogram (mass), second (time), ampere (current), kelvin (temperature), candela (luminous intensity), mole (amount of substance).
Significant figures: all certain digits plus the first uncertain digit. In multiplication/division, the result keeps as many significant figures as the quantity with the least.
Errors: absolute error = |measured value - true value|; relative error = absolute error / true value; percentage error = relative error x 100.
Dimensions express a quantity in terms of [M], [L], [T] etc. Example: force = [M L T^-2], energy = [M L^2 T^-2], pressure = [M L^-1 T^-2].
Dimensional analysis checks an equation's consistency and converts units, but it cannot find dimensionless constants like 1/2 or 2pi.
Least count: vernier callipers LC = 1 MSD - 1 VSD (commonly 0.01 cm); screw gauge LC = pitch / number of circular scale divisions (commonly 0.001 cm).
Parallax method measures large distances: D = b / theta, where b is the baseline and theta the parallax angle in radians.

questions.q: What is the dimensional formula of energy?
questions.a: Energy has dimensions [M L^2 T^-2], the same as work and torque.

questions.q: A measurement is recorded as 2.340 cm using a vernier callipers of least count 0.01 cm. How many significant figures?
questions.a: Four significant figures (2, 3, 4, 0). The trailing zero after the decimal counts because it shows the precision of the instrument.

questions.q: The period of a pendulum depends on length l and g. Using dimensions, find the form of T.
questions.a: T = k x sqrt(l/g), where k is a dimensionless constant (actually 2pi). T proportional to l^(1/2) g^(-1/2).

questions.q: Convert 1 N into dyne using dimensional analysis.
questions.a: 1 N = 10^5 dyne, since 1 kg = 10^3 g and 1 m = 10^2 cm, so 1 kg m/s^2 = 10^5 g cm/s^2.

chapters.title: Motion in a Straight Line
points: Displacement is the shortest straight-line change in position (a vector); distance is the total path length (a scalar). Displacement can be zero or negative, distance cannot.
Average velocity = displacement / time; instantaneous velocity v = dx/dt. Average speed = total distance / total time.
Acceleration a = dv/dt; the area under a velocity-time graph gives displacement; the slope of a position-time graph gives velocity.
Equations of uniformly accelerated motion: v = u + at; s = ut + (1/2)at^2; v^2 = u^2 + 2as.
Distance covered in the nth second: s_n = u + (a/2)(2n - 1).
For free fall under gravity, a = g = 9.8 m/s^2 downward; a body thrown up reaches max height h = u^2/(2g) in time t = u/g.
Relative velocity of A w. B is v_AB = v_A - v_B (in one dimension with signs).

questions.q: A car travels 100 m in 5 s from rest with uniform acceleration. Find its acceleration.
A ball is thrown vertically up at 20 m/s. Find the maximum height reached (g = 10 m/s^2).
What does the area under an acceleration-time graph give?
questions.a: It gives the change in velocity (delta v) over that time interval.

questions.q: A body covers equal distances in equal intervals of time in straight line motion. What can you say?
questions.a: It moves with uniform (constant) velocity, so its acceleration is zero.

chapters.title: Motion in a Plane
points: A vector has magnitude and direction. Resultant of two vectors: R = sqrt(A^2 + B^2 + 2AB cos theta); direction tan phi = B sin theta / (A + B cos theta).
Dot product A. B = AB cos theta (scalar, used for work); cross product |A x B| = AB sin theta (vector, used for torque), direction by right-hand rule.
Projectile motion: time of flight T = 2u sin theta / g; max height H = u^2 sin^2 theta / (2g); range R = u^2 sin 2theta / g. Range is maximum at theta = 45 degrees.
Uniform circular motion: centripetal acceleration a = v^2/r = omega^2 r, directed towards the centre; period T = 2pi/omega.
For a projectile, horizontal velocity stays constant (no horizontal acceleration) while vertical velocity changes under gravity.
Unit vectors i, j, k have magnitude 1 along x, y, z axes; any vector A = A_x i + A_y j + A_z k with |A| = sqrt(A_x^2 + A_y^2 + A_z^2).

questions.q: A projectile is fired at 30 m/s at 30 degrees to the horizontal. Find its range (g = 10 m/s^2).
questions.a: R = u^2 sin 2theta / g = 900 x sin 60 / 10 = 90 x 0.866 = 77.9 m (about 78 m).

questions.q: Two vectors of magnitudes 3 and 4 act at 90 degrees to each other. Find the resultant.
questions.a: R = sqrt(3^2 + 4^2) = 5 units, at an angle tan^-1(4/3) = 53 degrees from the 3-unit vector.

questions.q: Why is the work done by centripetal force zero?
questions.a: Centripetal force is always perpendicular to the displacement (tangent), so the dot product F. s = Fs cos 90 = 0.

questions.q: At what angle is the range of a projectile equal for two different projections?
questions.a: For complementary angles theta and (90 - theta), sin 2theta is the same, so the ranges are equal.

chapters.title: Laws of Motion
points: Newton's first law: a body resists change in its state of rest or uniform motion (law of inertia). Inertia increases with mass.
Newton's second law: F = dp/dt = ma. Momentum p = mv. Impulse = F x t = change in momentum.
Newton's third law: action and reaction are equal, opposite, and act on different bodies, so they never cancel each other.
Conservation of linear momentum: in the absence of external force, total momentum of a system stays constant (used in collisions and recoil).
Friction: static friction is self-adjusting up to f_max = mu_s N; kinetic friction f_k = mu_k N, with mu_k < mu_s. Friction opposes relative motion or its tendency.
Centripetal force needed for circular motion: F = mv^2/r. On a banked road the safe speed without friction is v = sqrt(rg tan theta).
Weight in a lift: apparent weight increases when the lift accelerates up (R = m(g + a)) and decreases when it accelerates down (R = m(g - a)); in free fall the person feels weightless.

questions.q: A 2 kg body moving at 5 m/s is stopped in 0.1 s. Find the average retarding force.
questions.a: Impulse = change in momentum = 2 x 5 = 10 kg m/s. F = 10 / 0.1 = 100 N.

questions.q: A gun of mass 10 kg fires a bullet of 0.05 kg at 200 m/s. Find the recoil velocity of the gun.
questions.a: By momentum conservation: 10 x V = 0.05 x 200 = 10, so V = 1 m/s opposite to the bullet.

questions.q: Why are roadways banked at curves?
questions.a: Banking tilts the normal reaction so its horizontal component provides the centripetal force, reducing dependence on friction and tyre wear.

questions.q: A block rests on a surface with mu_s = 0.5. Find the angle of repose.
questions.a: Angle of repose theta = tan^-1(mu_s) = tan^-1(0.5) = about 26.6 degrees.

chapters.title: Work, Energy and Power
points: Work W = F. s = Fs cos theta. Work is a scalar; it is zero if force or displacement is zero or if they are perpendicular.
Work-energy theorem: net work done on a body = change in its kinetic energy, W = (1/2)mv^2 - (1/2)mu^2.
Kinetic energy K = (1/2)mv^2 = p^2/(2m). Doubling speed makes K four times.
Potential energy: gravitational U = mgh near Earth's surface; spring potential energy = (1/2)kx^2; spring force F = -kx (Hooke's law).
Conservative forces (gravity, spring) do work independent of path; for them mechanical energy (K + U) is conserved when no other force does work.
Power P = W/t = F. v. 1 horsepower = 746 W.
Collisions: in elastic collisions both momentum and KE are conserved; in perfectly inelastic collisions bodies stick together and KE loss is maximum (momentum still conserved).

questions.q: A force of 10 N displaces a body by 5 m at 60 degrees to the force. Find the work done.
questions.a: W = Fs cos theta = 10 x 5 x cos 60 = 50 x 0.5 = 25 J.

questions.q: A 1 kg body falls freely from 10 m. Find its kinetic energy just before hitting the ground (g = 10 m/s^2).
questions.a: By energy conservation, K = mgh = 1 x 10 x 10 = 100 J.

questions.q: If the momentum of a body is doubled, what happens to its kinetic energy?
questions.a: K = p^2/(2m), so doubling p makes K four times the original.

questions.q: A motor lifts 200 kg of water to 10 m in 20 s. Find its power (g = 10 m/s^2).

chapters.title: System of Particles and Rotational Motion
points: Centre of mass of two particles: x_cm = (m1x1 + m2x2)/(m1 + m2). External force moves the CM as if all mass were concentrated there: F_ext = M a_cm.
Torque tau = r x F, magnitude rF sin theta. Angular momentum L = r x p = I omega; tau = dL/dt.
Moment of inertia I = sum m_i r_i^2. Ring: MR^2; disc: (1/2)MR^2; solid sphere: (2/5)MR^2; rod about centre: ML^2/12 (all about central axes through CM).
Rotational KE = (1/2) I omega^2. Total KE of a rolling body = (1/2)Mv_cm^2 + (1/2)I_cm omega^2.
Parallel axis theorem: I = I_cm + Md^2. Perpendicular axis theorem (for a plane lamina): I_z = I_x + I_y.
Angular momentum is conserved when net external torque is zero (e.g. a spinning skater speeds up by pulling arms in).
Rolling without slipping: v_cm = R omega, a_cm = R alpha. A solid sphere rolls down an incline faster than a ring because more of its energy is translational.

questions.q: Two masses 2 kg and 3 kg are placed at x = 1 m and x = 4 m. Find the centre of mass.
Find the moment of inertia of a disc of mass 2 kg and radius 0.5 m about its central axis.
A torque of 10 N m acts on a wheel of I = 2 kg m^2. Find its angular acceleration.
questions.a: alpha = tau/I = 10/2 = 5 rad/s^2.

questions.q: Why does a ballet dancer spin faster when she folds her arms?
questions.a: Folding arms reduces the moment of inertia; since angular momentum L = I omega is conserved, omega increases.

chapters.title: Gravitation
points: Newton's law of gravitation: F = G m1 m2 / r^2, with G = 6.67 x 10^-11 N m^2/kg^2. The force is always attractive.
Acceleration due to gravity: g = GM/R^2 at the surface. At height h: g' = g (R/(R+h))^2; at depth d: g' = g (1 - d/R). g decreases both ways.
Gravitational potential energy U = -GMm/r (zero at infinity). Potential V = -GM/r.
Orbital velocity of a satellite near Earth's surface v_o = sqrt(gR) = about 7.9 km/s. Escape velocity v_e = sqrt(2GM/R) = sqrt(2) x v_o = about 11.2 km/s.
Kepler's laws: planets move in ellipses with the Sun at one focus; areal velocity is constant; T^2 is proportional to r^3 (T^2/r^3 = constant).
A geostationary satellite has period 24 h, orbits in the equatorial plane at about 35,800 km height, and appears fixed in the sky.
Weightlessness in an orbiting satellite is due to free fall: satellite and everything inside fall towards Earth with the same acceleration g.

questions.q: Find the escape velocity from Earth if orbital velocity near the surface is 7.9 km/s.
questions.a: v_e = sqrt(2) x v_o = 1.414 x 7.9 = about 11.2 km/s.

questions.q: At what height above Earth's surface does g become one-fourth of its surface value?
questions.a: g' = g(R/(R+h))^2 = g/4 gives R+h = 2R, so h = R = 6400 km.

questions.q: State Kepler's third law.
questions.a: The square of the orbital period of a planet is directly proportional to the cube of the semi-major axis of its orbit: T^2 proportional to r^3.

questions.q: Why is there no atmosphere on the Moon?
questions.a: The Moon's escape velocity (about 2.3 km/s) is less than the rms speed of gas molecules at its surface temperature, so gases escaped over time.

chapters.title: Mechanical Properties of Solids
points: Stress = restoring force / area (N/m^2 or pascal). Strain = change in dimension / original dimension (no unit).
Hooke's law: within the elastic limit, stress is proportional to strain. Young modulus Y = longitudinal stress / longitudinal strain = (F/A) / (delta L / L).
Bulk modulus B = -P / (delta V / V) (negative sign because volume decreases as pressure increases). Shear modulus G = shear stress / shear strain.
Poisson ratio = lateral strain / longitudinal strain (typically 0.2-0.4 for metals; theoretical limits -1 to 0.5).
The stress-strain curve: proportional limit, elastic limit, yield point, ultimate tensile strength, fracture point. Area under it gives energy stored per unit volume.
Elastic potential energy stored in a stretched wire = (1/2) x stress x strain x volume = (1/2) F x delta L.

questions.q: A wire of length 2 m and area 1 mm^2 stretches by 1 mm under a load. Find the strain.
questions.a: Strain = delta L / L = 0.001 / 2 = 5 x 10^-4 (dimensionless).

questions.q: Steel has Young modulus 2 x 10^11 N/m^2. A stress of 10^8 N/m^2 is applied. Find the strain produced.
Why are steel girders used in bridges rather than aluminium of the same size?
questions.a: Steel has a much higher Young modulus and higher ultimate strength, so it deforms less under load and carries greater stress before failure.

questions.q: What is the SI unit of Young modulus?
questions.a: Pascal (N/m^2) - the same as stress, since strain is dimensionless.

chapters.title: Mechanical Properties of Fluids
points: Pascal's law: pressure applied to an enclosed fluid is transmitted equally in all directions (basis of the hydraulic lift: F2/F1 = A2/A1).
Pressure at depth h in a liquid: P = P_atm + rho g h. Pressure depends only on depth and density, not on the container's shape.
Archimedes' principle: upthrust = weight of liquid displaced = rho_liquid x V_submerged x g. A body floats when upthrust balances its weight.
Equation of continuity for incompressible flow: A1v1 = A2v2 - fluid speeds up in narrower sections.
Bernoulli's theorem (for steady, incompressible, non-viscous flow): P + (1/2) rho v^2 + rho g h = constant along a streamline.
Viscosity: Newton's law F = -eta A (dv/dx). Stokes' law for a sphere: F = 6 pi eta r v; terminal velocity v_t = 2r^2 (rho - sigma) g / (9 eta).
Surface tension S = F/l = energy per unit area. Excess pressure inside a liquid drop = 2S/R; inside a soap bubble = 4S/R. Capillary rise h = 2S cos theta / (rho g r).

questions.q: Find the pressure at a depth of 10 m in water (rho = 1000 kg/m^3, g = 10 m/s^2, atmospheric pressure 10^5 Pa).
questions.a: P = 10^5 + 1000 x 10 x 10 = 2 x 10^5 Pa (about 2 atmospheres).

questions.q: A soap bubble has twice the radius of another. Compare the excess pressure inside them.
questions.a: Excess pressure = 4S/R, inversely proportional to R. The bigger bubble has half the excess pressure of the smaller one (ratio 1:2).

questions.q: Why does a deep-sea diver wear a special suit?
questions.a: Pressure increases by about 1 atmosphere every 10 m of depth, so at great depths the huge water pressure would crush the body; the suit balances it.

questions.q: Water flows at 2 m/s through a pipe of area 4 cm^2 into a section of area 2 cm^2. Find the new speed.
questions.a: By continuity A1v1 = A2v2: 4 x 2 = 2 x v2, so v2 = 4 m/s.

chapters.title: Thermal Properties of Matter
points: Temperature scales: T(K) = t(deg C) + 273.15. Size of 1 degree is the same on Celsius and Kelvin scales.
Thermal expansion: linear delta L = alpha L delta T; area expansion coefficient beta = 2 alpha; volume expansion gamma = 3 alpha. For gases at constant pressure, gamma = 1/273 per degree C (ideal).
Specific heat capacity c: Q = m c delta T. Molar heat capacity uses moles. Water has a very high specific heat (4186 J/kg K), hence its use as a coolant.
Latent heat: Q = mL (no temperature change during phase change). Latent heat of fusion of ice = 3.34 x 10^5 J/kg; of vaporisation of water = 22.6 x 10^5 J/kg.
Heat transfer: conduction (Q/t = kA delta T / d), convection (fluid movement), radiation (Stefan-Boltzmann law P = sigma A T^4; Kirchhoff's law - good absorbers are good emitters).
Newton's law of cooling: rate of cooling is proportional to the excess temperature of the body over surroundings (for small differences).
Wien's displacement law: lambda_max x T = 2.9 x 10^-3 m K - hotter bodies radiate at shorter wavelengths.

questions.q: How much heat is needed to raise 0.5 kg of water from 20 deg C to 60 deg C? (c = 4200 J/kg K)
A metal rod of length 1 m expands by 1.2 mm when heated by 100 deg C. Find alpha.
questions.a: alpha = delta L / (L delta T) = 0.0012 / (1 x 100) = 1.2 x 10^-5 per degree C.

questions.q: Why does steam cause more severe burns than boiling water?
questions.a: Steam carries extra latent heat of vaporisation (about 22.6 x 10^5 J/kg) which it releases on condensing on the skin, in addition to cooling from 100 deg C.

questions.q: Two rods of same material but lengths 1 m and 2 m are heated equally. Which expands more in length?
questions.a: The 2 m rod expands twice as much in absolute length, since delta L is proportional to original length L (strain is the same for both).

chapters.title: Thermodynamics
points: Zeroth law: if A and B are each in thermal equilibrium with C, they are in equilibrium with each other - this defines temperature.
First law: delta Q = delta U + delta W (heat supplied = increase in internal energy + work done BY the gas). Sign convention: work done by gas is positive.
Isothermal process (T constant): delta U = 0, W = nRT ln(V2/V1). Adiabatic process (Q = 0): PV^gamma = constant, W = (P1V1 - P2V2)/(gamma - 1).
Molar heat capacities: C_p - C_v = R; gamma = C_p/C_v = 1.67 (monoatomic), 1.4 (diatomic), 1.33 (triatomic non-linear approx).
Second law (Kelvin-Planck): no engine can convert all heat into work. Carnot efficiency eta = 1 - T_cold/T_hot (temperatures in kelvin); it is the maximum possible.
Refrigerator COP = Q_cold / W = T_cold / (T_hot - T_cold) for a Carnot refrigerator.
Internal energy of an ideal gas depends only on temperature; for n moles of a gas with f degrees of freedom, U = (f/2) nRT.

questions.q: A gas absorbs 500 J of heat and does 200 J of work. Find the change in internal energy.
questions.a: delta U = delta Q - delta W = 500 - 200 = 300 J.

questions.q: Find the efficiency of a Carnot engine working between 400 K and 300 K.
In an adiabatic expansion, a gas does work. What happens to its temperature?
questions.a: With Q = 0, the work comes from internal energy, so U and hence temperature decrease - the gas cools.

questions.q: For a monoatomic ideal gas, what are C_v and C_p?

chapters.title: Kinetic Theory
points: Ideal gas equation: PV = nRT = Nk_B T. Pressure from kinetic theory: P = (1/3) rho c_rms^2 = (2/3) x (KE per unit volume).
rms speed c_rms = sqrt(3RT/M) = sqrt(3k_B T/m). Average KE of one molecule = (3/2) k_B T; per mole = (3/2) RT.
Degrees of freedom: monoatomic gas f = 3 (translational); diatomic at room temperature f = 5 (3 translational + 2 rotational). Equipartition: each degree of freedom carries (1/2) k_B T per molecule.
Law of equipartition links internal energy U = (f/2) nRT and heat capacities C_v = (f/2) R, C_p = (f/2 + 1) R.
Mean free path lambda = 1 / (sqrt(2) pi d^2 N/V): increases when density decreases or molecule size decreases.
Maxwell speed distribution: most probable speed = sqrt(2RT/M), average speed = sqrt(8RT/(pi M)), rms speed = sqrt(3RT/M); rms is the largest of the three.

questions.q: Find the rms speed of oxygen molecules at 300 K (M = 0.032 kg/mol, R = 8.31 J/mol K).
What is the average kinetic energy of a gas molecule at 300 K? (k_B = 1.38 x 10^-23 J/K)
At what temperature will the rms speed of hydrogen molecules equal that of oxygen at 300 K?
questions.a: c_rms proportional to sqrt(T/M). For equal speeds T_H2 / M_H2 = T_O2 / M_O2, so T_H2 = 300 x (2/32) = 18.75 K.

questions.q: How many degrees of freedom does a diatomic gas have at room temperature?
questions.a: Five: 3 translational and 2 rotational (vibrational modes are inactive at room temperature).

chapters.title: Oscillations
points: SHM: displacement x = A sin(omega t + phi); acceleration a = -omega^2 x (always directed to mean position); velocity v = omega sqrt(A^2 - x^2).
Time period T = 2pi/omega; frequency nu = 1/T. For a spring-mass system T = 2pi sqrt(m/k); for a simple pendulum T = 2pi sqrt(l/g).
Energy in SHM: KE = (1/2) m omega^2 (A^2 - x^2), PE = (1/2) m omega^2 x^2; total E = (1/2) m omega^2 A^2 stays constant (no friction).
KE and PE are equal at x = A/sqrt(2). At the mean position KE is maximum and PE minimum; at extremes the reverse.
Phase: two oscillators with phase difference 0 are in phase; pi means opposite phase. Phase difference = (2pi/lambda) x path difference in waves.

Damped oscillations lose amplitude gradually due to friction; forced oscillations take the driver's frequency; resonance occurs when driver frequency equals natural frequency, giving maximum amplitude.

questions.q: A simple pendulum has length 1 m. Find its time period (g = 9.8 m/s^2).
questions.a: T = 2pi sqrt(l/g) = 2pi sqrt(1/9.8) = about 2.0 s (a 'seconds pendulum').

questions.q: A particle in SHM has amplitude 5 cm and period 2 s. Find its maximum velocity.
questions.a: v_max = A omega = 0.05 x (2pi/2) = 0.05pi = 0.157 m/s.

questions.q: A mass of 0.5 kg on a spring of k = 50 N/m oscillates. Find the frequency.
questions.a: nu = (1/2pi) sqrt(k/m) = (1/2pi) sqrt(100) = 10/(2pi) = about 1.59 Hz.

questions.q: At what displacement is the KE of an SHM particle half its total energy?

chapters.title: Waves
points: Wave speed v = nu x lambda. Transverse waves (light, strings) vibrate perpendicular to propagation; longitudinal waves (sound) vibrate parallel, forming compressions and rarefactions.
Progressive wave equation: y = A sin(omega t - kx + phi), where k = 2pi/lambda is the propagation constant.
Speed of a transverse wave on a stretched string v = sqrt(T/mu), where T is tension and mu is mass per unit length.
Speed of sound in a gas (Newton-Laplace): v = sqrt(gamma P / rho) = sqrt(gamma RT / M). Sound speed in air is about 332 m/s at 0 deg C and increases about 0.61 m/s per degree C rise.

Standing waves: nodes (zero amplitude) and antinodes (maximum amplitude) form. String fixed at both ends: harmonics nu_n = n v/(2L), all harmonics present. Open organ pipe: all harmonics; closed pipe: only odd harmonics, fundamental nu = v/(4L).
Beats: when two sounds of close frequencies nu1 and nu2 play together, beat frequency = |nu1 - nu2|.
Doppler effect: apparent frequency changes when source and observer move relative to each other; frequency increases on approach, decreases on recession.

questions.q: A wave of frequency 500 Hz travels at 350 m/s. Find its wavelength.
questions.a: lambda = v/nu = 350/500 = 0.7 m.

questions.q: Two tuning forks of 256 Hz and 260 Hz sound together. How many beats per second are heard?
questions.a: Beat frequency = |260 - 256| = 4 beats per second.

questions.q: A string of length 1 m and mass 5 g is under tension 80 N. Find the wave speed on it.
questions.a: mu = 0.005 kg/m. v = sqrt(T/mu) = sqrt(80/0.005) = sqrt(16000) = about 126.5 m/s.

questions.q: A closed organ pipe and an open pipe have the same length. Compare their fundamental frequencies.
questions.a: Closed pipe fundamental = v/(4L); open pipe = v/(2L). The open pipe's fundamental is twice that of the closed pipe.

chapters.title: Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry
points: Laws of chemical combination: law of conservation of mass (Lavoisier), law of definite proportions (Proust), law of multiple proportions (Dalton), Gay-Lussac's law of gaseous volumes, Avogadro's law.
1 mole = 6.022 x 10^23 entities (Avogadro number) = molar mass in grams. Number of moles n = given mass / molar mass = given particles / N_A.
Empirical formula is the simplest whole-number ratio; molecular formula = n x empirical formula, where n = molar mass / empirical formula mass.
Percentage composition = (mass of element / molar mass) x 100. Limiting reagent is the reactant consumed first and decides the amount of product.
Concentration terms: molarity M = moles of solute / litres of solution; molality m = moles of solute / kg of solvent; mole fraction = moles of component / total moles.
Stoichiometry uses the balanced equation's mole ratio: 2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O means 2 mol H2 reacts with 1 mol O2.
Dalton's atomic theory: atoms are indestructible particles of an element; compounds form by combining atoms in simple whole-number ratios.

questions.q: How many molecules are present in 11 g of CO2? (M = 44 g/mol)
Find the empirical formula of a compound with 40% C, 6.7% H and 53.3% O.
Define the limiting reagent with an example.
questions.a: The reactant used up first, which limits product formation. If 3 mol H2 and 1 mol O2 react (2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O), O2 is the limiting reagent and only 2 mol H2O forms.

questions.q: What is the molarity of a solution containing 8 g NaOH in 500 mL solution? (M = 40 g/mol)
questions.a: Moles = 8/40 = 0.2 mol; volume = 0.5 L; M = 0.2/0.5 = 0.4 mol/L.

chapters.title: Structure of Atom
points: Discovery: electron by Thomson (cathode rays, e/m measured), proton by Goldstein (anode rays), neutron by Chadwick (1932).

Rutherford's alpha-scattering: atom has a tiny dense positive nucleus; most mass is in the nucleus, most of the atom is empty space. Limitation: cannot explain stability (orbiting electrons should radiate and spiral in).
Bohr's model: electrons revolve in fixed orbits with angular momentum mvr = n h/(2pi). Energy of nth orbit for H: E_n = -13.6 / n^2 eV. Radius r_n = 0.529 x n^2 Angstrom for H.
Bohr's model fails for multi-electron atoms and cannot explain spectral line splitting in magnetic fields (Zeeman effect).
de Broglie: every particle has wavelength lambda = h/(mv). Heisenberg uncertainty: delta x x delta p >= h/(4pi) - position and momentum cannot both be known exactly.
Quantum numbers: n (principal: size/energy), l (azimuthal: shape of subshell, 0 to n-1), m (magnetic: orientation, -l to +l), s (spin: +1/2 or -1/2).

Aufbau principle (fill increasing n+l), Pauli exclusion (no two electrons share all 4 quantum numbers), Hund's rule (degenerate orbitals fill singly first). s, p, d, f subshells hold 2, 6, 10, 14 electrons.
Half-filled and fully filled subshells are extra stable: Cr is [Ar] 3d^5 4s^1 and Cu is [Ar] 3d^10 4s^1 instead of the expected configurations.

questions.q: What are the quantum numbers of the outermost electron of sodium (Z = 11)?
questions.a: Configuration: 1s^2 2s^2 2p^6 3s^1. The 3s electron has n = 3, l = 0, m = 0, s = +1/2.

questions.q: Calculate the energy of the electron in the second orbit of hydrogen.
Why is copper's configuration [Ar] 3d^10 4s^1 and not [Ar] 3d^9 4s^2?
questions.a: A completely filled d subshell (3d^10) is extra stable, so one 4s electron moves into 3d.

questions.q: How many orbitals and electrons can the M shell (n = 3) hold?
questions.a: Orbitals = n^2 = 9; maximum electrons = 2n^2 = 18.

chapters.title: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
points: Modern periodic law: properties of elements are periodic functions of their atomic numbers (Moseley).
Long form of the periodic table: 7 periods (rows) and 18 groups (columns). Blocks: s (groups 1-2), p (13-18), d (transition metals), f (lanthanides/actinides).
Atomic radius decreases across a period (increasing effective nuclear charge pulls electrons in) and increases down a group (new shells are added).
Ionisation enthalpy: energy to remove an electron; increases across a period, decreases down a group. Be and N are higher than expected due to stable filled/half-filled subshells.

Electron gain enthalpy: energy released on adding an electron; generally increases across a period; chlorine has the highest (more than fluorine because F is very small and electron repulsion offsets attraction).
Electronegativity: tendency to attract shared electrons; increases across a period, decreases down a group; fluorine is the most electronegative element.
Diagonal relationship: Li resembles Mg, Be resembles Al (similar charge density) because trends oppose each other across and down.

questions.q: Arrange Na, Mg, Al in increasing order of ionisation enthalpy and explain.
questions.a: Na < Mg < Al in first ionisation enthalpy, because effective nuclear charge increases across the period, holding electrons more tightly.

questions.q: Which has a larger atomic radius: K or Br? Why?
questions.a: Potassium is much larger; radius increases down a group and decreases across a period, and K is both to the left and lower than Br.

questions.q: Why does chlorine have a higher electron gain enthalpy than fluorine?
questions.a: Fluorine is extremely small, so electron-electron repulsion in its compact 2p subshell offsets the attraction; Cl (3p) accepts the extra electron more easily.

questions.q: Name the most electronegative element and the element with the highest electron gain enthalpy.
questions.a: Most electronegative: fluorine (F). Highest electron gain enthalpy: chlorine (Cl).

chapters.title: Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure
points: Ionic bond: complete electron transfer from metal to non-metal; lattice energy holds the crystal (e.g. NaCl). Conducts electricity only in molten/aqueous state.
Covalent bond: electron sharing; formed by orbital overlap - sigma bonds (axial overlap, stronger) and pi bonds (sideways overlap).

VSEPR theory: electron pairs arrange to minimise repulsion; lone pair-lone pair > lone pair-bond pair > bond pair-bond pair repulsion. Shapes: linear (2 bp), trigonal planar (3), tetrahedral (4), e. NH3 is pyramidal and H2O is bent due to lone pairs.
Hybridisation: sp (linear, 180 deg, e. CO2), sp2 (trigonal planar, 120 deg, e. BF3), sp3 (tetrahedral, 109.5 deg, e. CH4).
Molecular orbital theory: bonding MOs lower energy, antibonding MOs raise it; bond order = (N_b - N_a)/2. Bond order zero means no stable molecule.
Dipole moment measures bond polarity; molecules with symmetric shapes (CO2, CCl4) have zero net dipole. Hydrogen bonding (H bonded to F, O, N) gives water and ice their special properties.
Resonance: delocalised electrons shown by multiple Lewis structures (e. benzene, O3); the true structure is a hybrid with bond lengths between single and double.

questions.q: Predict the shape of NH3 and explain using VSEPR.
questions.a: Nitrogen has 3 bond pairs and 1 lone pair (4 electron domains, tetrahedral arrangement), but the lone pair compresses the angles, giving a pyramidal shape with 107 degree bond angle.

questions.q: What are the hybridisation and shape of BF3?
questions.a: Boron has 3 bond pairs and no lone pair: sp2 hybridisation, trigonal planar shape, 120 degree angles.

questions.q: Find the bond order of O2 (16 electrons total).
questions.a: Configuration gives 10 bonding and 6 antibonding electrons: bond order = (10 - 6)/2 = 2, a double bond.

questions.q: Why does H2O have a bent shape while CO2 is linear?
questions.a: H2O has 2 bond pairs plus 2 lone pairs, which repel and bend the molecule (104.5 deg); CO2 has only 2 bond pairs, which take the linear 180 deg arrangement.

chapters.title: Thermodynamics
points: System types: open (exchanges matter and energy), closed (energy only), isolated (neither). State functions (U, H, S, G) depend only on the state, not the path; heat and work are path functions.
First law: delta U = q + w (chemistry sign convention: work done ON the system is positive). Enthalpy H = U + PV; at constant pressure delta H = q_p.
Enthalpy changes: delta_f H (formation), delta_c H (combustion), Hess's law (delta H of a reaction is the sum of delta H of its steps, independent of path).
Bond enthalpies estimate delta H: sum of (bonds broken) minus sum of (bonds formed).
Entropy S measures disorder; delta S = q_rev / T. Spontaneous processes increase total entropy of the universe.
Gibbs free energy: delta G = delta H - T delta S. Reaction is spontaneous when delta G < 0; at equilibrium delta G = 0 and delta G = -RT ln K.
A reaction is always spontaneous when delta H < 0 and delta S > 0; it becomes spontaneous at high temperature when delta H > 0 and delta S > 0 (T > delta H / delta S).

questions.q: For a reaction, delta H = -100 kJ/mol and delta S = -200 J/mol K. Is it spontaneous at 300 K?
questions.a: delta G = delta H - T delta S = -100,000 - 300(-200) = -100,000 + 60,000 = -40,000 J = -40 kJ < 0, so yes, spontaneous.

questions.q: State Hess's law and give its use.
questions.a: The enthalpy change of a reaction is the same whether it occurs in one step or many steps. It lets us find delta H for reactions that cannot be measured directly, using known steps.

questions.q: Why does ice melt spontaneously above 0 deg C?
questions.a: Melting increases entropy (delta S > 0); above the melting point T delta S exceeds delta H of fusion, making delta G negative.

questions.q: In which case does work by the system on surroundings have a negative sign in chemistry convention?
questions.a: Work done BY the system on the surroundings is taken as negative in the chemistry sign convention (delta U = q + w), because the system loses energy.

chapters.title: Equilibrium
points: Dynamic equilibrium: forward and reverse rates are equal; concentrations stay constant though reactions continue (e., in a closed vessel H2 + I2 <=> 2HI).
Law of mass action: for aA + bB <=> cC + dD, K_c = [C]^c [D]^d / ([A]^a [B]^b). K_p uses partial pressures; K_p = K_c (RT)^(delta n).
Reaction quotient Q compares with K: if Q < K the reaction moves forward; if Q > K it moves backward; Q = K at equilibrium.

Le Chatelier's principle: a system at equilibrium shifts to oppose any change - increasing reactant concentration, pressure (towards fewer gas moles), or lowering temperature for exothermic reactions favours products.
Acids donate H+ (Bronsted-Lowry) or accept electron pairs (Lewis); conjugate acid-base pairs differ by one H+. Water is amphiprotic.
pH = -log [H+]; pOH = -log [OH-]; at 25 deg C pH + pOH = 14 and K_w = 10^-14. Buffer solutions resist pH change (weak acid + its salt, or weak base + its salt).
Solubility product K_sp: for a sparingly soluble salt, precipitation occurs when the ionic product exceeds K_sp (common ion effect lowers solubility).

questions.q: For N2 + 3H2 <=> 2NH3, how does increasing pressure affect the equilibrium?
questions.a: The product side has 2 gas moles vs 4 on the reactant side, so higher pressure shifts equilibrium towards NH3 (fewer gas molecules).

questions.q: The pH of a solution is 4. Find [H+].
A reaction has K_c = 10 and Q_c = 2 at some moment. Which direction will it proceed?
questions.a: Q < K, so the forward reaction proceeds until Q rises to K.

questions.q: What is the pH of 0.01 M NaOH solution?

chapters.title: Redox Reactions
points: Oxidation = loss of electrons (increase in oxidation number); reduction = gain of electrons (decrease in oxidation number). They always occur together.

Oxidation number rules: free elements 0; Group 1 metals +1; Group 2 +2; F -1; O usually -2 (except -1 in peroxides, +2 in OF2); H usually +1 (except -1 in metal hydrides). Sum of oxidation numbers equals the charge of the species.
Oxidising agents accept electrons (get reduced): e. KMnO4, K2Cr2O7. Reducing agents donate electrons (get oxidised): e. metals, H2, C.

Balancing redox reactions: ion-electron (half-reaction) method - split into oxidation and reduction halves, balance atoms (O with H2O, H with H+ in acidic medium), balance charge with electrons, then combine.
Disproportionation: the same element is both oxidised and reduced (e. Cl2 + 2NaOH -> NaCl + NaOCl + H2O; here Cl goes from 0 to -1 and +1).
Electrochemical series: metals above hydrogen displace H2 from acids; a metal higher in the series displaces one below it from its salt solution.

questions.q: Find the oxidation number of Cr in K2Cr2O7.
Identify the oxidising and reducing agents in: Zn + CuSO4 -> ZnSO4 + Cu.
questions.a: Zn is oxidised (0 to +2), so Zn is the reducing agent; Cu2+ is reduced (+2 to 0), so CuSO4 is the oxidising agent.

questions.q: Balance: Fe2+ + Cr2O7^2- -> Fe3+ + Cr3+ (acidic medium).
questions.a: Half reactions: Cr2O7^2- + 14H+ + 6e- -> 2Cr3+ + 7H2O; Fe2+ -> Fe3+ + e- (x6). Combined: Cr2O7^2- + 14H+ + 6Fe2+ -> 2Cr3+ + 7H2O + 6Fe3+.

questions.q: Is this disproportionation? 2H2O2 -> 2H2O + O2.
questions.a: Yes: oxygen goes from -1 in H2O2 to -2 in H2O (reduction) and to 0 in O2 (oxidation).

chapters.title: Organic Chemistry - Some Basic Principles and Techniques
points: Tetravalency of carbon (Kekule) and catenation: carbon forms 4 covalent bonds and long chains, giving millions of organic compounds.
Functional groups decide a compound's chemistry: -OH (alcohol), -CHO (aldehyde), -CO- (ketone), -COOH (carboxylic acid), -NH2 (amine), -X (halide).
IUPAC naming: choose the longest chain containing the principal functional group, number to give it the lowest locant; prefixes for substituents in alphabetical order (e., 2-methylbutane).
Structural isomerism: chain (butane vs 2-methylpropane), position (1-propanol vs 2-propanol), functional (ethanol vs dimethyl ether), metamerism, tautomerism (keto-enol).
Electronic effects: inductive effect (electronegativity-based, permanent), electromeric effect (temporary, on attack), resonance/mesomeric effect (delocalisation), hyperconjugation.
Carbocation stability: 3 deg > 2 deg > 1 deg (hyperconjugation + inductive); carbanion stability is the reverse. Free radicals follow carbocation order.
Purification: distillation (liquids), fractional distillation, crystallisation (solids), chromatography, sublimation (e. camphor), steam distillation for steam-volatile compounds.
Qualitative analysis: Lassaigne's test - N gives Prussian blue, S gives violet with nitroprusside, halogens give AgX precipitate. Quantitative: Kjeldahl (N), Carius (halogen/S).

questions.q: Write the IUPAC name of CH3-CH(CH3)-CH2-CH3.
questions.a: The longest chain has 4 carbons with a methyl at position 2: 2-methylbutane.

questions.q: Arrange in increasing carbocation stability: (CH3)3C+, (CH3)2CH+, CH3CH2+.
questions.a: CH3CH2+ < (CH3)2CH+ < (CH3)3C+, i., 1 deg < 2 deg < 3 deg, due to increasing hyperconjugation.

questions.q: What is the difference between inductive and electromeric effects?
questions.a: Inductive effect is the permanent polarisation of sigma bonds by electronegative atoms; the electromeric effect is a temporary shift of pi electrons under the attack of a reagent.

questions.q: How would you separate a mixture of camphor and common salt?
questions.a: By sublimation: camphor sublimes to vapour on gentle heating and condenses on a cool surface, leaving salt behind.

chapters.title: Hydrocarbons
points: Alkanes (CnH2n+2): saturated, sp3. Preparation: hydrogenation of alkenes/alkynes, Wurtz reaction (2RX + 2Na -> R-R), decarboxylation of sodium salts (soda lime: RCOONa + NaOH -> RH). Reactions: free-radical halogenation (reactivity 3 deg > 2 deg > 1 deg H), combustion, pyrolysis/cracking.

Alkenes (CnH2n): contain C=C, sp2. Preparation: dehydration of alcohols (conc. H2SO4, Saytzeff product major), dehydrohalogenation of alkyl halides. Reactions: electrophilic addition - H2, X2, HX (Markovnikov: H adds to the carbon with more H already), hydration, ozonolysis (cleaves double bond).

Alkynes (CnH2n-2): C triple C, sp. Acetylene from CaC2 + H2O. Terminal alkynes are acidic (pKa about 25): RC triple CH + NaNH2 -> salt; gives red precipitate with ammoniacal Cu2Cl2 and white with AgNO3. Addition of HX twice (Markovnikov), hydration gives methyl ketones (Hg2+/H2SO4).

Benzene: aromatic, planar hexagon with delocalised pi electrons; Huckel rule (4n+2 pi electrons) explains stability. Electrophilic substitution: nitration (conc. HNO3 + conc. H2SO4 -> nitrobenzene), halogenation (FeX3), sulphonation, Friedel-Crafts alkylation/acylation (AlCl3).
Directing effects: -OH, -NH2, -CH3 are ortho/para directors and activators; -NO2, -CHO, -COOH are meta directors and deactivators (halogens are ortho/para but deactivating).
Conformations of ethane: staggered is more stable than eclipsed (torsional strain); energy difference about 12.5 kJ/mol. Sawhorse and Newman projections show them.
Markovnikov's rule explained by the most stable carbocation intermediate; peroxide effect (Kharasch) reverses it only for HBr addition.

questions.q: Convert ethyne to benzene.
questions.a: Pass ethyne through a red-hot iron tube at 873 K: 3 HC triple CH -> C6H6 (cyclic polymerisation).

questions.q: Predict the major product of propene + HBr.
questions.a: Markovnikov addition: H adds to C1 (the carbon with more H), Br to C2, giving 2-bromopropane as the major product.

questions.q: How do you distinguish 1-butyne from 2-butyne?
questions.a: 1-butyne is a terminal alkyne with an acidic H: it gives a red precipitate with ammoniacal cuprous chloride; 2-butyne does not react.

questions.q: Why does benzene undergo substitution rather than addition?
questions.a: Addition would destroy the delocalised aromatic sextet (losing resonance stabilisation); substitution keeps the aromatic ring intact, so it is energetically preferred.

chapters.title: Sets
points: A set is a well-defined collection of distinct objects. Roster form lists elements: A = {1, 2, 3}; set-builder form: A = {x : x is a natural number less than 4}.
Subsets: A is a subset of B if every element of A is in B. A set with n elements has 2^n subsets and 2^n - 1 proper subsets. Power set P(A) is the set of all subsets.
Operations: union A u B, intersection A n B, difference A - B, complement A' (elements of universal set not in A).
De Morgan's laws: (A u B)' = A' n B'; (A n B)' = A' u B'.
For finite sets: n(A u B) = n(A) + n(B) - n(A n B); n(A u B u C) = n(A) + n(B) + n(C) - n(A n B) - n(B n C) - n(C n A) + n(A n B n C).
Intervals: open (a, b), closed [a, b], half-open [a, b). Empty set phi has zero elements and is a subset of every set.

questions.q: If A = {1, 2} and B = {2, 3, 4}, find A u B and A n B.
A set has 5 elements. How many subsets does it have?
questions.a: 2^5 = 32 subsets (31 proper subsets).

questions.q: In a class, 25 students like cricket, 20 like football, and 10 like both. How many like at least one?
questions.a: n(C u F) = 25 + 20 - 10 = 35 students.

questions.q: State De Morgan's first law and verify with A = {1, 2}, B = {2, 3}, U = {1, 2, 3, 4}.
questions.a: (A u B)' = {4}; A' n B' = {3, 4} n {1, 4} = {4}. Both equal, so the law holds.

chapters.title: Relations and Functions
points: Ordered pair (a, b): order matters. Cartesian product A x B = {(a, b) : a in A, b in B}; if n(A) = p and n(B) = q, then n(A x B) = pq.
Relation R from A to B is a subset of A x B. Domain = set of first elements; range = set of second elements.
Function f: A -> B assigns each element of A exactly one element of B. Domain, co-domain, range: range is a subset of the co-domain.
Types: one-one (injective: distinct inputs give distinct outputs), onto (surjective: range = co-domain), one-one onto (bijective).
Standard functions: identity f(x) = x; constant f(x) = c; polynomial; rational; modulus f(x) = |x|; signum; greatest integer f(x) = [x].
Algebra of functions: (f + g)(x) = f(x) + g(x), (fg)(x) = f(x)g(x), (f/g)(x) = f(x)/g(x) where g(x) is not zero.

questions.q: Is the relation {(1, 2), (1, 3), (2, 4)} a function? Why?
questions.a: No, because the input 1 has two different outputs (2 and 3); a function needs exactly one output per input.

questions.q: Find the domain of f(x) = 1/(x - 2).
questions.a: The denominator cannot be zero, so x is not 2: domain = all real numbers except 2.

questions.q: Check whether f(x) = 2x + 1 from R to R is one-one and onto.
questions.a: If f(a) = f(b) then 2a + 1 = 2b + 1 gives a = b, so one-one. For any real y, x = (y-1)/2 maps to y, so onto. It is bijective.

questions.q: Find the range of f(x) = x^2 + 1, x real.
questions.a: x^2 >= 0 for all real x, so f(x) >= 1: range = [1, infinity).

chapters.title: Trigonometric Functions
points: Angle in radians = arc length / radius; 1 radian = 57.3 degrees (approx). 360 deg = 2pi radians; to convert: radians = degrees x pi/180.
ASTC rule by quadrant: I (all positive), II (sin positive), III (tan positive), IV (cos positive). sin(-x) = -sin x; cos(-x) = cos x; tan(-x) = -tan x.
Key identities: sin^2 x + cos^2 x = 1; 1 + tan^2 x = sec^2 x; 1 + cot^2 x = cosec^2 x.
Compound angles: sin(A+B) = sin A cos B + cos A sin B; cos(A+B) = cos A cos B - sin A sin B; tan(A+B) = (tan A + tan B)/(1 - tan A tan B).
Double angles: sin 2A = 2 sin A cos A; cos 2A = cos^2 A - sin^2 A = 2cos^2 A - 1 = 1 - 2sin^2 A; tan 2A = 2 tan A/(1 - tan^2 A).
Product to sum: 2 sin A cos B = sin(A+B) + sin(A-B); 2 cos A sin B = sin(A+B) - sin(A-B); cos^2 A = (1 + cos 2A)/2.
Sum to product: sin C + sin D = 2 sin((C+D)/2) cos((C-D)/2); cos C + cos D = 2 cos((C+D)/2) cos((C-D)/2).

questions.q: Find the exact value of sin 75 degrees.
questions.a: sin 75 = sin(45 + 30) = sin45 cos30 + cos45 sin30 = (sqrt6 + sqrt2)/4.

questions.q: If tan x = 3/4 and x is in the third quadrant, find sin x.
questions.a: In quadrant III sin is negative: sin x = -3/5 (from 3-4-5 triangle).

questions.q: Prove that cos 2A = 1 - 2 sin^2 A.
questions.a: cos 2A = cos^2 A - sin^2 A = (1 - sin^2 A) - sin^2 A = 1 - 2 sin^2 A.

questions.q: Simplify: (sin 2x)/(1 + cos 2x).
questions.a: sin 2x = 2 sin x cos x and 1 + cos 2x = 2 cos^2 x, so the ratio = tan x.

chapters.title: Complex Numbers and Quadratic Equations
points: i = sqrt(-1), with i^2 = -1, i^3 = -i, i^4 = 1. A complex number z = a + ib has real part a and imaginary part b; modulus |z| = sqrt(a^2 + b^2).
Conjugate of a + ib is a - ib; z x conjugate(z) = |z|^2. To divide, multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate.
Argand plane: real axis (x) and imaginary axis (y); z = a + ib is the point (a, b); |z| is its distance from origin.
Argument theta = tan^-1(b/a) (adjusted by quadrant). Polar form: z = r(cos theta + i sin theta), where r = |z|.
Algebra: (a+ib) + (c+id) = (a+c) + i(b+d); (a+ib)(c+id) = (ac - bd) + i(ad + bc).
Quadratic ax^2 + bx + c = 0 has roots x = (-b +- sqrt(b^2 - 4ac)) / (2a). Discriminant D = b^2 - 4ac: D > 0 two real roots; D = 0 equal roots; D < 0 complex conjugate roots.
Sum of roots = -b/a, product of roots = c/a. A quadratic with roots alpha, beta is x^2 - (sum)x + (product) = 0.

questions.q: Simplify (2 + 3i) / (1 - i).
Find the modulus and argument of 1 + i sqrt3.
questions.a: |z| = sqrt(1 + 3) = 2. Argument = tan^-1(sqrt3) = 60 deg (pi/3), since both parts are positive.

questions.q: Solve x^2 + 4x + 13 = 0.
Form a quadratic equation with roots 2 and -5.
questions.a: Sum = -3, product = -10, so x^2 + 3x - 10 = 0.

chapters.title: Linear Inequalities
points: Inequality rules: adding/subtracting the same number keeps the sense; multiplying/dividing by a positive number keeps it, by a negative number reverses it.
Solving ax + b > 0: e. 2x - 6 > 0 gives x > 3. Solution sets are intervals on the number line.
Quadratic inequalities: factor and use a sign chart. x^2 - 4 > 0 gives x < -2 or x > 2.
Absolute value: |x| < a means -a < x < a; |x| > a means x < -a or x > a.
Two-variable inequalities ax + by > c: the boundary line ax + by = c divides the plane; test the origin to find the solution half-plane.
System of inequalities: solution is the intersection (common region) of all individual solution sets, found graphically.

questions.q: Solve: 3x + 5 < 2x + 11.
questions.a: Subtracting 2x and 5: x < 6.

questions.q: Solve: x^2 - 9 <= 0.
questions.a: (x-3)(x+3) <= 0, which holds between the roots: -3 <= x <= 3.

questions.q: Solve: |2x - 1| < 5.
Solve: -4x + 8 >= 0.
questions.a: Dividing by -4 reverses the inequality: x <= 2.

chapters.title: Permutations and Combinations
points: Fundamental principle of counting: if one task has m ways and another has n ways, both together have m x n ways.
Factorial: n! = n(n-1)...2x1; 0! = 1. Permutations (order matters): nPr = n! / (n-r)!; combinations (order irrelevant): nCr = n! / (r!(n-r)!).
nPr counts arrangements (seating, passwords); nCr counts selections (committees, teams).
Key results: nCr = nC(n-r); nC0 = nCn = 1; nC1 = n; nCr + nC(r-1) = (n+1)Cr (Pascal's rule).
Permutations of n objects with p, q identical among them: n! / (p! q!).
Circular arrangements: (n-1)! for n distinct objects around a circle.

questions.q: How many 3-digit numbers can be formed from digits 1-6 without repetition?
In how many ways can a committee of 4 be chosen from 10 people?
How many arrangements of the letters of MISSISSIPPI are possible?
How many ways can 5 people sit around a round table?

chapters.title: Binomial Theorem
points: Binomial theorem: (a + b)^n = sum over r of nCr a^(n-r) b^r, for r = 0 to n. There are n+1 terms.
General term: T_(r+1) = nCr a^(n-r) b^r. Middle term(s): if n is even, the ((n/2)+1)th term; if n is odd, two middle terms.
Coefficients are symmetric: nCr = nC(n-r). Sum of all binomial coefficients = 2^n.
(1 + x)^n = 1 + nx + nC2 x^2 + ...; putting x = 1 and x = -1 gives useful coefficient sums.
Greatest binomial coefficient: for even n it is nC(n/2); for odd n both nC((n-1)/2) and nC((n+1)/2).

questions.q: Find the 4th term in the expansion of (x + 2)^6.
Find the coefficient of x^5 in (x + 1/x)^10.
questions.a: General term: 10Cr x^(10-r) (1/x)^r = 10Cr x^(10-2r). For x^5: 10 - 2r = 5 gives r = 2.5, not an integer - no such term, coefficient 0.

questions.q: Find the middle term of (2x - 1/x)^6.
questions.a: n = 6 is even, middle term is T_4 = 6C3 (2x)^3 (-1/x)^3 = 20 x 8x^3 x (-1/x^3) = -160.

questions.q: Evaluate (1.02)^5 approximately using binomial expansion (first three terms).

chapters.title: Sequences and Series
points: Arithmetic progression: a, a+d, a+2d...; nth term a_n = a + (n-1)d; sum S_n = (n/2)(2a + (n-1)d) = (n/2)(first + last).
Geometric progression: a, ar, ar^2...; nth term a_n = a r^(n-1); sum S_n = a(r^n - 1)/(r - 1). For |r| < 1, infinite sum S_inf = a/(1 - r).
Arithmetic mean of a and b: (a+b)/2. Geometric mean: sqrt(ab). AM >= GM for positive numbers.
Relation between AM, GM, HM: AM >= GM >= HM; GM^2 = AM x HM.
Special sums: sum k = n(n+1)/2; sum k^2 = n(n+1)(2n+1)/6; sum k^3 = [n(n+1)/2]^2.
A series converges to a finite sum only if its terms tend to zero (necessary but not sufficient); the infinite GP sum formula needs |r| < 1.

questions.q: Find the 20th term of the AP 5, 9, 13, ...
Find the sum of the first 12 terms of the GP 3, 6, 12, ...
Find the sum to infinity of 1 + 1/2 + 1/4 + ...
The AM of two numbers is 10 and GM is 8. Find the numbers.
questions.a: Let the numbers be a, b: a+b = 20, ab = 64. Solving t^2 - 20t + 64 = 0 gives t = 4 or 16: the numbers are 4 and 16.

chapters.title: Straight Lines
points: Slope m = tan theta = (y2 - y1)/(x2 - x1), where theta is the angle with the positive x-axis. Parallel lines have equal slopes; perpendicular lines have m1 x m2 = -1.
Forms: point-slope y - y1 = m(x - x1); slope-intercept y = mx + c; two-point form; intercept form x/a + y/b = 1; normal form x cos alpha + y sin alpha = p.
General equation: Ax + By + C = 0 has slope -A/B and intercepts (-C/A, -C/B).
Angle between lines with slopes m1, m2: tan theta = |(m1 - m2)/(1 + m1 m2)|.
Distance of point (x1, y1) from line Ax + By + C = 0: d = |Ax1 + By1 + C| / sqrt(A^2 + B^2). Distance between parallel lines differs only in C.
Concurrency: three lines are concurrent if they pass through one point; check using determinants or by solving two and substituting in the third.

questions.q: Find the slope of the line joining (2, 5) and (6, 13).
Find the equation of the line through (3, -2) with slope 4.
Find the distance of (4, 1) from the line 3x - 4y + 5 = 0.
Find the angle between the lines y = 2x + 1 and y = -3x + 5.

chapters.title: Conic Sections
points: Circle: (x - h)^2 + (y - k)^2 = r^2. General form x^2 + y^2 + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0 has centre (-g, -f) and radius sqrt(g^2 + f^2 - c).
Parabola: set of points equidistant from focus and directrix; standard form y^2 = 4ax (focus (a, 0), directrix x = -a).
Ellipse: x^2/a^2 + y^2/b^2 = 1 (a > b); foci at (+-c, 0) with c^2 = a^2 - b^2; eccentricity e = c/a < 1; latus rectum = 2b^2/a.
Hyperbola: x^2/a^2 - y^2/b^2 = 1; foci at (+-c, 0) with c^2 = a^2 + b^2; e > 1; asymptotes y = +- (b/a)x.
Eccentricity identifies the conic: e = 0 circle, e = 1 parabola, 0 < e < 1 ellipse, e > 1 hyperbola.
Parametric points: circle (r cos theta, r sin theta); ellipse (a cos theta, b sin theta).

questions.q: Find the centre and radius of x^2 + y^2 - 4x + 6y - 3 = 0.
questions.a: Centre = (2, -3); radius = sqrt(4 + 9 + 3) = sqrt(16) = 4.

questions.q: Find the focus of the parabola y^2 = 12x.
questions.a: Compare with y^2 = 4ax: 4a = 12 gives a = 3, so focus = (3, 0).

questions.q: Find the eccentricity of the ellipse 9x^2 + 25y^2 = 225.
A conic has eccentricity 1.5. Which conic is it?
questions.a: e > 1 means a hyperbola.

chapters.title: Introduction to Three Dimensional Geometry
points: A point in 3D is (x, y, z): x, y, z are distances from the YZ, XZ, XY planes respectively. The eight octants are the 3D analogue of quadrants.
Distance between (x1, y1, z1) and (x2, y2, z2): sqrt((x2-x1)^2 + (y2-y1)^2 + (z2-z1)^2).
Distance of (x, y, z) from the origin: sqrt(x^2 + y^2 + z^2). Distance from coordinate planes: |x| from YZ, |y| from XZ, |z| from XY.
Section formula: point dividing the join of (x1,y1,z1) and (x2,y2,z2) in ratio m:n is ((mx2+nx1)/(m+n), (my2+ny1)/(m+n), (mz2+nz1)/(m+n)); midpoint uses m = n = 1.
Centroid of triangle with vertices (x1,y1,z1), (x2,y2,z2), (x3,y3,z3): the average of the coordinates.

questions.q: Find the distance between (1, 2, 3) and (4, 6, 8).
questions.a: d = sqrt(9 + 16 + 25) = sqrt(50) = 5 sqrt2 units.

questions.q: Find the midpoint of A(2, -1, 5) and B(6, 3, -1).
In which octant does (-2, 3, -5) lie?
questions.a: x negative, y positive, z negative: the octant with signs (-, +, -).

questions.q: Find the point dividing A(1, 2, 3) and B(7, 8, 9) in the ratio 2:1.

chapters.title: Limits and Derivatives
points: Limit: lim x->a f(x) = L means f(x) approaches L as x approaches a. Direct substitution works when the function is continuous there.
Standard limits: lim x->0 sin x / x = 1; lim x->0 (e^x - 1)/x = 1; lim x->0 (a^x - 1)/x = ln a; lim x->0 (1+x)^(1/x) = e; lim x->a (x^n - a^n)/(x - a) = n a^(n-1).
Algebra of limits: limit of sum/product/quotient = sum/product/quotient of limits (denominator not zero). Factorise or rationalise to remove 0/0 forms.
Derivative: f'(x) = lim h->0 [f(x+h) - f(x)]/h (first principle). Geometrically it is the slope of the tangent at that point.
Rules: (x^n)' = n x^(n-1); (u+v)' = u' + v'; (uv)' = u'v + uv'; (u/v)' = (u'v - uv')/v^2; chain rule dy/dx = dy/du x du/dx.
Derivatives of trig functions: (sin x)' = cos x; (cos x)' = -sin x; (tan x)' = sec^2 x.

questions.q: Evaluate lim x->0 (sin 5x)/x.
questions.a: Write as 5 x (sin 5x)/(5x); the bracket tends to 1, so the limit = 5.

questions.q: Evaluate lim x->2 (x^2 - 4)/(x - 2).
Find the derivative of f(x) = x^3 - 5x^2 + 7 from first principles or rules.
Find the derivative of (x^2 + 1)(x^3 - 2x).

chapters.title: Statistics
points: Measures of central tendency: mean, median, mode. Measures of dispersion: range, mean deviation, variance, standard deviation.
Mean deviation about mean = (sum |x_i - xbar|) / n; about median uses median in place of mean.
Variance sigma^2 = (sum (x_i - xbar)^2) / n = (sum x_i^2)/n - (xbar)^2. Standard deviation sigma = sqrt(variance).
For grouped data: mean = sum f_i x_i / sum f_i; variance = (sum f_i x_i^2 / N) - (mean)^2.
Coefficient of variation CV = (sigma / xbar) x 100: smaller CV means more consistent data - used to compare two series.
Standard deviation is independent of origin (shifting data doesn't change it) but scales with change of scale: if y = ax + b, sigma_y = |a| sigma_x.

questions.q: Find the mean deviation about the mean for 2, 4, 6, 8, 10.
questions.a: Mean = 6. Deviations: 4, 2, 0, 2, 4; sum = 12; MD = 12/5 = 2.4.

questions.q: Find the variance of 1, 2, 3, 4, 5.
Two series have (mean 20, SD 2) and (mean 30, SD 3). Which is more consistent?
questions.a: CV1 = (2/20)x100 = 10%, CV2 = (3/30)x100 = 10%: equally consistent.

questions.q: If each observation is increased by 5, what happens to the standard deviation?
questions.a: No change: standard deviation is independent of a shift of origin.

chapters.title: Probability
points: Random experiment: outcome not predictable in advance. Sample space S = set of all possible outcomes; an event is a subset of S.
Probability of event E: P(E) = n(E) / n(S) for equally likely outcomes; 0 <= P(E) <= 1; P(impossible) = 0, P(sure) = 1.
Complement: P(not E) = 1 - P(E). Addition rule: P(A u B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A n B); for mutually exclusive events P(A u B) = P(A) + P(B).
Mutually exclusive events cannot occur together (A n B = phi); exhaustive events cover the whole sample space.
For two dice: sample space has 36 outcomes; P(sum = 7) = 6/36 = 1/6; P(doublet) = 6/36 = 1/6.
P(at least one) = 1 - P(none) is often the fastest route in 'at least' problems.

questions.q: A card is drawn from a 52-card deck. Find P(king).
questions.a: 4 kings in 52 cards: P = 4/52 = 1/13.

questions.q: Two dice are thrown. Find P(sum = 10).
questions.a: Favourable: (4,6), (5,5), (6,4) = 3 outcomes out of 36: P = 3/36 = 1/12.

questions.q: P(A) = 0.4, P(B) = 0.5, P(A n B) = 0.2. Find P(A u B).
A bag has 5 red and 3 black balls. One ball is drawn. Find P(not red).

chapters.title: The Living World
points: Defining properties of living beings: growth, reproduction, metabolism, cellular organisation and consciousness (ability to sense the environment).
Biodiversity: about 1.7-1.8 million species have been identified and described so far; many more await discovery.
Taxonomy is the classification, identification and nomenclature of organisms. Systematics also includes evolutionary relationships (Linnaeus is called the father of taxonomy).

Binomial nomenclature (Carolus Linnaeus): each name has two parts - genus (capital first letter) and specific epithet (lowercase). Names are in Latin, written in italics (or underlined when handwritten).
Taxonomic hierarchy (broad to narrow): Kingdom > Phylum/Division > Class > Order > Family > Genus > Species. Species is the basic unit; taxa with fewer ranks share more common features.
Example: mango - Kingdom Plantae, Division Angiospermae, Class Dicotyledonae, Order Sapindales, Family Anacardiaceae, Genus Mangifera, Species indica.

questions.q: Who proposed binomial nomenclature and what are its two components?
questions.a: Carolus Linnaeus. The two components are the generic name (genus) and the specific epithet, e. Homo sapiens.

questions.q: Arrange the hierarchy in ascending order: Family, Phylum, Species, Class.
questions.a: Species < Family < Class < Phylum (species is the smallest, most specific category).

questions.q: Why is reproduction alone not a defining property of life?
questions.a: Some organisms like mules, worker bees and infertile couples cannot reproduce, yet they are alive. Defining properties must hold for all living beings.

questions.q: What is the scientific name of housefly and man?
questions.a: Housefly: Musca domestica. Man: Homo sapiens.

chapters.title: Biological Classification
points: R. Whittaker (1969) proposed the five-kingdom system: Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae, Animalia - based on cell structure, body organisation, nutrition and phylogeny.

Monera: prokaryotic bacteria; cell wall has peptidoglycan. Includes archaebacteria (extreme habitats), eubacteria (true bacteria), cyanobacteria (photosynthetic, e. Nostoc, Anabaena - nitrogen fixers).

Protista: single-celled eukaryotes - Chrysophytes (diatoms, golden algae; chief ocean producers), Dinoflagellates (e. Gonyaulax causes red tides), Euglenoids (Euglena - mixotroph), Slime moulds, Protozoans (Amoeba, Paramoecium, Plasmodium - malarial parasite).
Fungi: eukaryotic, heterotrophic, cell wall of chitin. Classes: Phycomycetes (Mucor), Ascomycetes (yeast, Penicillium), Basidiomycetes (Agaricus mushroom), Deuteromycetes (Alternaria).

Viruses are non-cellular, obligate intracellular parasites with protein coat (capsid); they are inert outside a host - not placed in the five-kingdom system. Viroids (Diener) are naked RNA; prions are infectious proteins; lichens are symbiosis of alga + fungus.

questions.q: Name the five kingdoms in Whittaker's classification.
questions.a: Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia.

questions.q: Which organism is responsible for red tides and which group does it belong to?
questions.a: Gonyaulax, a dinoflagellate (Protista). Its rapid multiplication colours the sea red.

questions.q: How do lichens indicate air pollution?
questions.a: Lichens do not grow in polluted areas (high SO2), so their presence/absence signals pollution levels - they are pollution indicators.

questions.q: Give two differences between viruses and bacteria.
questions.a: Viruses are non-cellular, have only DNA or RNA (never both) and are inert outside hosts; bacteria are cellular prokaryotes that can live independently and have both DNA and RNA.

chapters.title: Plant Kingdom
points: Algae: chlorophyllous simple plants, mostly aquatic. Green algae (Chlamydomonas, Spirogyra), brown algae (Laminaria, Fucus - contain fucoxanthin), red algae (Polysiphonia, Gelidium - source of agar).
Algae provide at least half of the Earth's total CO2 fixation through photosynthesis.

Bryophytes: amphibians of the plant kingdom (need water for fertilisation); no true vascular tissue; main plant body is haploid gametophyte. Examples: Funaria (moss), Marchantia (liverwort), Sphagnum (peat moss).
Pteridophytes: first terrestrial plants with vascular tissue (xylem and phloem); main body is diploid sporophyte; seedless. Examples: Selaginella, Equisetum (horsetail), ferns like Dryopteris.
Gymnosperms: naked seeds (ovules not enclosed in an ovary). Examples: Pinus, Cycas (living fossil), Ginkgo. Male and female cones are borne on the same or different plants.
Angiosperms: seeds enclosed in fruits; divided into dicots (two cotyledons, reticulate venation) and monocots (one cotyledon, parallel venation). Flowers are the reproductive units.
Life cycles: haplontic (e. Volvox), diplontic (e. Fucus, seed plants), haplo-diplontic (bryophytes, pteridophytes, e. Ectocarpus); all show alternation of generations.

questions.q: Why are bryophytes called the amphibians of the plant kingdom?
questions.a: They live on land (soil) but depend on water for sexual reproduction, because their male gametes must swim to the egg, just like amphibians return to water to breed.

questions.q: From which alga is agar obtained and what is it used for?
questions.a: Agar is obtained from Gelidium and Gracilaria (red algae). It is used to grow microbes and in ice creams and jellies.

questions.q: Give two differences between gymnosperms and angiosperms.
questions.a: Gymnosperms have naked seeds not enclosed in a fruit and no flowers; angiosperms have ovules inside an ovary forming fruits, and bear flowers. Gymnosperms lack vessels in xylem (except few) and companion cells.

questions.q: Name the dominant phase in the life cycle of a moss and a fern.
questions.a: Moss: the dominant free-living phase is the haploid gametophyte. Fern: the dominant phase is the diploid sporophyte.

chapters.title: Animal Kingdom
points: Basis of classification: level of organisation, body symmetry, germ layers, coelom, segmentation, notochord.
Symmetry: asymmetrical (sponges), radial (coelenterates, ctenophores, adult echinoderms), bilateral (most animals from Platyhelminthes onwards).
Body cavity (coelom): acoelomates (Platyhelminthes), pseudocoelomates (Aschelminthes, e. Ascaris), coelomates (Annelida onwards).

Key phyla with NCERT examples: Porifera (Sycon, Spongilla), Coelenterata/Cnidaria (Hydra, Aurelia - jellyfish), Ctenophora (Pleurobrachia), Platyhelminthes (Taenia - tapeworm, Planaria), Aschelminthes (Ascaris, Wuchereria - filarial worm), Annelida (Pheretima - earthworm, Hirudinaria - leech), Arthropoda (largest phylum; Apis, Bombyx), Mollusca (Pila, Octopus), Echinodermata (Asterias - starfish), Hemichordata (Balanoglossus), Chordata.
Chordate features: notochord, dorsal hollow nerve cord, pharyngeal gill slits, post-anal tail (at some stage). Vertebrates have the notochord replaced by a vertebral column.
Arthropoda is the largest animal phylum (over 2/3 of named species); jointed appendages and chitinous exoskeleton are its features.

questions.q: What is metamerism? Give an example.
questions.a: True segmentation where the body is divided into repeating segments (metameres), internally and externally, as in the earthworm (Annelida).

questions.q: Name two parasitic adaptations in Platyhelminthes.
questions.a: They have hooks and suckers for attachment to hosts, and the body is covered by a tough tegument; digestive system is incomplete or absent since they absorb digested food from the host.

questions.q: How can you distinguish chordates from non-chordates?
questions.a: Chordates have a notochord (at some stage of life), a dorsal hollow single nerve cord, paired pharyngeal gill slits and a post-anal tail; non-chordates lack these and have a solid ventral nerve cord.

questions.q: Water canal system is characteristic of which phylum? How does it help?
questions.a: Phylum Porifera (sponges). Water enters through ostia into the spongocoel and exits via osculum, helping in food gathering, respiration and waste removal.

chapters.title: Morphology of Flowering Plants
points: Root systems: tap root (from radicle, e. mustard, dicots) vs fibrous root (from base of stem, e. wheat, monocots). Modifications: storage (carrot, turnip), prop roots (banyan), stilt roots (maize, sugarcane), pneumatophores for breathing (Rhizophora).

Stem modifications: tendrils (cucumber), thorns (Citrus, Bougainvillea), underground storage (potato - tuber, ginger - rhizome, onion - bulb, Colocasia - corm), runner (grass), stolon (jasmine), offset (Eichhornia), sucker (banana).

Leaf: parts - leaf base, petiole, lamina. Venation: reticulate (dicots) vs parallel (monocots). Phyllotaxy: alternate, opposite, whorled. Modifications: tendril (pea), spines (cactus), storage (onion), insect capture (pitcher plant).
Inflorescence: racemose (main axis keeps growing, younger flowers at top) vs cymose (main axis ends in a flower, older at top).

Flower: bisexual/unisexual; actinomorphic (radial symmetry, mustard) vs zygomorphic (bilateral, pea, gulmohur); ovary position: hypogynous (superior ovary, mustard), perigynous (plum, rose), epigynous (inferior ovary, guava, cucumber).

Aestivation: valvate (Calotropis), twisted (china rose), imbricate (Cassia), vexillary (pea). Placentation: marginal (pea), axile (tomato, lemon), parietal (mustard, Argemone), basal (sunflower), free central (Primrose).
Floral formula uses symbols: Br (bracteate), K (calyx), C (corolla), A (androecium), G (gynoecium); floral diagrams represent flower structure.

questions.q: How do roots of Rhizophora help the plant?
questions.a: Rhizophora grows in swampy mangrove areas; its pneumatophores (breathing roots) grow vertically upward out of the mud to get oxygen for respiration.

questions.q: Differentiate racemose and cymose inflorescence.
questions.a: In racemose, the main axis continues to grow and flowers open in acropetal order (younger at apex); in cymose, the main axis ends in a flower, limiting growth, and flowers open in basipetal order.

questions.q: Which family shows vexillary aestivation and marginal placentation?
questions.a: Family Fabaceae (pea family) - vexillary (papilionaceous) corolla and marginal placentation in the ovary.

questions.q: Is potato a root or a stem? How can you tell?
questions.a: It is a modified stem (tuber): it has nodes ('eyes') with buds and scale leaves, which roots never have.

chapters.title: Anatomy of Flowering Plants
points: Tissue systems: epidermal (protection), ground tissue system (cortex, pith, pericycle), vascular tissue system (xylem + phloem in vascular bundles).
Simple tissues: parenchyma (living, thin walls, storage/photosynthesis), collenchyma (living, thickened corners, flexibility), sclerenchyma (dead, lignified walls, mechanical strength).

Complex tissues: xylem (tracheids, vessels, xylem parenchyma, xylem fibres - conducts water, mostly dead) and phloem (sieve tube elements, companion cells, phloem parenchyma, phloem fibres - translocates food).
Dicot stem: vascular bundles are conjoint, collateral and open (cambium present), arranged in a ring. Monocot stem: bundles are closed (no cambium) and scattered in ground tissue.
Dicot root: xylem and phloem in separate radial bundles (2-4 xylem arms). Monocot root: polyarch (many xylem bundles) with a large pith.

Dorsiventral (dicot) leaf: palisade mesophyll near upper surface, stomata mostly on lower surface, bundle sheath cells. Isobilateral (monocot) leaf: mesophyll not differentiated, bulliform cells in upper epidermis help leaf rolling.
Anomalous secondary growth aside, dicots show secondary growth by vascular cambium and cork cambium; monocots generally lack secondary growth.

questions.q: Why is secondary growth absent in monocot stems?
questions.a: Their vascular bundles are closed - there is no cambium between xylem and phloem, so no secondary xylem/phloem (wood) can be produced.

questions.q: Distinguish xylem vessels from tracheids.
questions.a: Vessels are long tube-like structures made of many cells with open (perforated) end walls, giving continuous water columns; tracheids are single elongated cells with tapering ends and intact walls, water passes through pits.

questions.q: What are bulliform cells and where are they found?
questions.a: Large, empty, colourless motor cells in the upper epidermis of grass (monocot) leaves; they lose water and make leaves curl in dry weather, reducing water loss.

questions.q: Compare dicot and monocot roots anatomically.
questions.a: Dicot root: 2-4 xylem bundles (diarch to tetrarch), small or absent pith, secondary growth occurs. Monocot root: more than 6 xylem bundles (polyarch), large well-developed pith, no secondary growth.

chapters.title: Structural Organisation in Animals
points: Four tissue types: epithelial, connective, muscular, neural.

Epithelial tissue lines surfaces: squamous (thin, in alveoli and blood vessels), cuboidal (kidney tubules, glands), columnar (stomach, intestine lining), ciliated columnar (fallopian tubes, bronchioles), glandular (secretion).

Connective tissues connect and support: loose (areolar, adipose), dense (tendons connect muscle to bone, ligaments connect bone to bone), specialised (cartilage, bone, blood - fluid connective tissue).

Muscular tissue: skeletal/striated (voluntary, attached to bones), smooth (involuntary, in digestive tract and blood vessels, spindle-shaped), cardiac (only in heart, striated but involuntary, with intercalated discs).
Neural tissue: neurons are the unit; neuroglia protect and support them. Neurons conduct impulses, but neuroglial cells make up more than half the volume of neural tissue.
Frog (Rana tigrina) is the NCERT model organism: cold-blooded, undergoes metamorphosis, males have vocal sacs and copulatory pads; heart is 3-chambered (2 atria, 1 ventricle).

questions.q: What is the function of intercalated discs in cardiac muscle?
questions.a: They are communication junctions that let adjacent cardiac muscle cells contract as one unit, so the heart beats in a coordinated wave without fatigue.

questions.q: How do tendons differ from ligaments?
questions.a: Tendons connect muscles to bones; ligaments connect bones to bones. Both are dense regular connective tissues rich in collagen.

questions.q: Why is blood called a fluid connective tissue?
questions.a: It has cells (RBC, WBC, platelets) suspended in a fluid matrix (plasma) and connects all body parts by transporting gases, nutrients, hormones and wastes.

questions.q: Mention two identifying features of male frogs.
questions.a: Male frogs have vocal sacs that amplify their croak, and a copulatory (nuptial) pad on the first digit of the forelimb to grip the female during mating.

chapters.title: Cell: The Unit of Life
points: Cell theory (Schleiden and Schwann, later refined by Virchow): all organisms are made of cells, the cell is the basic unit of life, and new cells arise from pre-existing cells (omnis cellula e cellula).
Prokaryotic cells (bacteria): no membrane-bound nucleus or organelles; DNA is a single circular molecule in the nucleoid; ribosomes are 70S; mesosomes are membrane infoldings.
Eukaryotic cells: true nucleus and organelles. Plant cells have a cell wall (cellulose), chloroplasts and a large central vacuole; animal cells lack walls and plastids but have centrioles.

Endomembrane system: ER (rough ER - protein synthesis with ribosomes; smooth ER - lipid synthesis), Golgi apparatus (packaging, modification, lysosome formation), lysosomes (suicidal bags with hydrolytic enzymes), vacuoles.
Mitochondria: double membrane, own DNA and 70S ribosomes, site of aerobic respiration (powerhouse of the cell). Chloroplast: double membrane with thylakoids stacked as grana, site of photosynthesis.

Cytoskeleton (microfilaments, microtubules, intermediate filaments) gives shape and movement. Nucleus contains chromatin (DNA + histones); nucleolus makes rRNA. Ribosomes (80S in eukaryotes = 60S + 40S) synthesise proteins.

questions.q: Why are lysosomes called 'suicidal bags' of the cell?
questions.a: They contain powerful hydrolytic enzymes; if the lysosomal membrane ruptures, these enzymes digest the cell itself, so they serve in destroying worn-out organelles and the cell in emergencies.

questions.q: Distinguish between rough and smooth endoplasmic reticulum.
questions.a: RER has ribosomes on its surface and synthesises/folds proteins (abundant in pancreatic cells); SER lacks ribosomes and synthesises lipids and detoxifies drugs (abundant in liver cells).

questions.q: What is the 9+2 arrangement in cilia and flagella?
questions.a: The axoneme of cilia/flagella has 9 pairs of peripheral microtubules surrounding 2 central microtubules, giving them their characteristic bending movement.

questions.q: Name the sites of (a) ATP synthesis and (b) rRNA synthesis in a eukaryotic cell.
questions.a: (a) Mitochondria (inner membrane/cristae). (b) Nucleolus inside the nucleus.

chapters.title: Biomolecules
points: Primary metabolites (proteins, carbohydrates, lipids, nucleic acids) have identifiable functions; secondary metabolites (alkaloids like morphine, codeine; pigments; drugs like vinblastin; essential oils) have no direct role in growth but many are useful to humans.

Carbohydrates: monosaccharides (glucose, fructose, ribose), disaccharides (sucrose = glucose + fructose; lactose = glucose + galactose; maltose = glucose + glucose), polysaccharides (starch - energy storage in plants, glycogen - animal starch, cellulose - structural, beta-1,4 links, gives no colour with iodine).

Proteins: polymers of amino acids joined by peptide bonds; 20 standard amino acids. Structure levels: primary (sequence), secondary (alpha helix, beta pleated sheet), tertiary (3D folding), quaternary (multiple chains, e. haemoglobin with 4 subunits). Collagen is the most abundant animal protein; RuBisCO is the most abundant protein in the biosphere.
Lipids: fatty acids + glycerol; saturated (no double bonds, solid) vs unsaturated (double bonds, liquid oils). Phospholipids form cell membranes.
Nucleic acids: nucleotides = nitrogenous base + pentose sugar + phosphate. DNA: 2'-deoxyribose, bases A, G, C, T. RNA: ribose (extra 2'-OH), U instead of T.

Enzymes are protein catalysts: lower activation energy, speed reactions without being consumed. Activity depends on temperature (optimum ~37 deg C) and pH; competitive inhibitors resemble the substrate (e. sulpha drugs, statins), non-competitive bind elsewhere. Apoenzyme + cofactor = holoenzyme.

questions.q: What type of bond links (a) amino acids in proteins and (b) nucleotides in nucleic acids?
questions.a: (a) Peptide bond (-CO-NH-) between the amino group of one amino acid and carboxyl group of another. (b) Phosphodiester bond between phosphate and sugars of successive nucleotides.

questions.q: Why does cellulose not give a blue colour with iodine while starch does?
questions.a: Iodine fits into the coiled helical structure of amylose in starch; cellulose has straight beta-linked chains with no helical coils to hold iodine, so no blue colour forms.

questions.q: How does a competitive inhibitor work, with an example?
questions.a: It competes for the enzyme's active site because it resembles the substrate. Example: sulphanilamide competes with PABA in bacterial folate synthesis, and statins competitively inhibit HMG-CoA reductase in cholesterol synthesis.

questions.q: What is the difference between a nucleotide and a nucleoside?
questions.a: A nucleoside = nitrogenous base + sugar. A nucleotide = nucleoside + phosphate group (attached to the 5' carbon of sugar).

chapters.title: Cell Cycle and Cell Division
points: Cell cycle: interphase (G1 - growth, S - DNA synthesis, G2 - preparation) + M phase (division). G0 is the quiescent exit phase (e. nerve cells, heart cells). Duration: about 24 h in human cells; yeast ~90 min.
DNA content doubles in the S phase but chromosome number stays the same. Cell cycle is about 95% interphase.

Mitosis stages: prophase (chromatin condenses, spindle forms), metaphase (chromosomes align at equator/metaphase plate), anaphase (sister chromatids separate to poles), telophase (nuclear envelope re-forms). Followed by cytokinesis (cell plate in plants, furrow in animals).
Significance of mitosis: growth, repair, cell replacement, maintaining chromosome number; basis of asexual reproduction.

Meiosis: two divisions - meiosis I (reductional: homologues separate, crossing over in prophase I) and meiosis II (equational: chromatids separate). Prophase I stages: leptotene, zygotene (synapsis, bivalents form), pachytene (crossing over at chiasmata), diplotene, diakinesis.

Crossing over between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes creates new gene combinations (variation) - the raw material for evolution. Meiosis produces 4 haploid cells from one diploid cell.

questions.q: A cell with 2n = 16 undergoes meiosis. How many chromosomes will each daughter cell have?
questions.a: Meiosis halves the number: each of the 4 daughter cells will have n = 8 chromosomes.

questions.q: In which stage of prophase I does crossing over occur, and what is exchanged?
questions.a: Crossing over occurs in the pachytene stage; non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes exchange corresponding segments at chiasmata, producing recombinant chromatids.

questions.q: Why is meiosis I called the reduction division?
questions.a: Because homologous chromosomes separate and move to opposite poles, reducing the chromosome number from diploid (2n) to haploid (n) in the daughter cells.

questions.q: If the DNA content of a cell in G1 is 2C, what is it at the end of the S phase and after mitosis?
questions.a: After the S phase it becomes 4C; after mitosis each daughter cell returns to 2C.

chapters.title: Photosynthesis in Higher Plants
points: Photosynthesis: 6CO2 + 12H2O --(light, chlorophyll)--> C6H12O6 + 6O2 + 6H2O. Oxygen released comes from water, not CO2 (proved by isotope experiments).
Site: chloroplast. Light reactions (in thylakoid membrane/grana) need light: photolysis of water, ATP and NADPH produced. Dark reactions (Calvin cycle, in stroma) use ATP and NADPH to fix CO2.
Pigments: chlorophyll a (chief pigment, blue-green), chlorophyll b, xanthophylls, carotenoids (accessory pigments that widen the absorption spectrum and protect against photo-oxidation).
Photosystems: PS II (P680) and PS I (P700). Non-cyclic photophosphorylation involves both and releases O2; cyclic flow involves only PS I (only ATP formed).
Calvin cycle (C3): CO2 acceptor is RuBP (5C); first stable product is 3-PGA (3C); cycle needs 18 ATP and 12 NADPH per glucose.
